utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Tuesday, February 2nd, 2010, and I first greet the members of the OTP in the courtroom, Mr. Seselj, and everyone helping us. In a few minutes, we will bring a witness in the courtroom. This witness has protective measures. Let me tell you right away that as far as next week is concerned, we were supposed to hear VS-034. Unfortunately, he will not come. He's ill. He has a health problem, so he will not be able to come next week. And we're trying to schedule him at another time. However, the week after that, February 16 and 17, we'll be hearing VS-067. He is available, but given his health, this will be a video conference. And on the week after, VS-0032, we also have a problem because he's also ill, so there will probably not be any hearing, given his health. We're also trying to reschedule him. However, the week after, March 2nd and 3rd, there's no problem, VS-017 is available. So as you see, we're confronted with health situations, and because of that we have to reschedule a number of witnesses. Mr. Seselj, I hope that you have noted down all of this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm just not clear on one thing, Mr. President. What does it mean to reschedule him for later? Is that a permanent illness or an acute infection and then we can put it off for a week, whereas reschedule him, well, who knows how long that can take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As of now, all -- the situation is very temporary. We're trying to postpone by a week. We are awaiting medical records to see whether the witness can actually travel or not. If he cannot travel, then we have to organise a video conference. But as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, we are doing our utmost to make sure that they come as soon as possible. Unfortunately, between what the Trial Chamber wishes and medical treatment, there is a problem. We just heard that a witness had just had surgery. Of course, because he just had surgery, he cannot travel, which is why we are running late or he is running late. This is the kind of problem that we are running into, but the schedule is as I just told you. Mr. Seselj, let me take this opportunity to ask you the following: Given the schedule for Court witnesses, at first glance, and it's just, you know, an estimation, we should be done with the Chamber witnesses or Court witnesses during the month of March, probably at the end of March, so we will no longer have any witnesses. I'd already asked you this question, but I will put it to you again. As far as Rule 98 bis is concerned, are you going to need any time between the end of the testimony of the last witness to prepare, or do you need no time for preparation, or do you just decide not to use Rule 98 bis?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've already said it on two occasions, that I will use that Rule, and two or three days will be sufficient for my preparations. So let's not lose even one week. When we finish with a witness within one week, to the following Tuesday that's enough for me, two or three days in between to prepare, and I can carry on and utilise Rule 98 bis, because it is my intention to go through the indictment on the basis of that Rule and to draw your attention to the fact that the Prosecutor has proved absolutely nothing of what he accuses me of. So we're not even going to lose a single working week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What you've said is very important. As soon as we're done with the last witness, we'll probably finish on a Wednesday, so you'll have Thursday, Friday, the weekend, and Monday to prepare, and we will immediately start with Rule 98 bis on the next Tuesday. Everything is clear. And that way, we will not waste any time. You told us on two occasions, and this is the third time that you're telling us, that you want to take the floor for Rule 98 bis, and I wanted this to be absolutely clear for each and every one here. Let's drop the blinds now and bring the witness into the courtroom. There's no one in the gallery, but still we have to abide by the Rules. And we will first move into closed session. Could you please move into closed session, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness VS-1067, you made two statements to the OTP, the first one on August 18 and 19, 1998, and the second one almost six years later on March 1st and 2nd, 2004. We have these statements. Could you please tell us, as far as -- could you tell me the following: The first time you met the OTP, what exactly happened? Did they call you, did they contact you? Could you tell me how you came into contact with them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Sir, you were detained in a country. The OTP then contacted you. You met them in the prison where you were being detained or did you meet them elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't meet them in prison. I had a meeting with them when I left prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You met them once you had been released. You spent two days with them, the 18th and 19th of August, 1998. Were there any questions and answers from you or was it just you giving a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only recounted what happened and how it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told them what had happened. When you told them what had happened, did the OTP investigator input all the information in his computer or was he taking down notes in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly. I don't remember whether he had a computer. But he did have a notebook, and he was writing things down in that notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 19th of August, to be precise, you were asked to sign your statement, which is a ten-page statement. This statement, which you were asked to sign, was it in English or was it in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in English, but there was an interpreter there who interpreted it, because, well, I guess there wasn't enough time for that person to write it down in our language. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you signed, did the interpreter interpret into your language those ten pages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And after that, you signed. So much for 1998. Then you meet the OTP again on the 2nd of March, 2004. Did they contact you once more or did you contact them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They got in contact with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When they contacted you, well, this lasted two days. This was for the 1st and 2nd of March, and you gave a much shorter statement, a five-page statement with 30 paragraphs, and I assume that you were then given the statement in English, you were asked to sign it, and then those five pages were translated back to you; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, but I know that there was an interpreter there, that she interpreted things to me. (redacted) (redacted). I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, line 2, page 10, you need to redact it, because he is saying which country the person putting questions to him came from. So last question on this: At any point in time in 1998 or in 2004, were you told that you were going to be testifying in Mr. Seselj's trial, or were you told nothing at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't say anything to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You weren't told anything. So in March 2004, you will go on with your job. This is going to be my last question. Since March 2004 until today, did Mr. Seselj or his associates phone you up at some point in time; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me on what day, which year, which month, and who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, he called me on 2007, I believe, in November, this little guy called Samardzic, Dragan Samardzic. He's from Mostar. He said that he'd kill my children this way, that way. He started talking nonsense, and I hung up. Three or four months later, Drago Tamindzija me and said that I had no business testifying there because I cannot say anything. I answered, Well, yes, there's nothing I can say that I don't already know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those two people who called you, how do you know that they are close to Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first one I mentioned, Dragan Samardzic, I didn't know on whose behalf he was calling at all. As for Mr. Drago Tamindzija, when I was in Nevesinje in 1996, he was a member of the Serb Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying as far as the first one is concerned, you don't know, but as far as the second one is concerned, you know that he was a member of the Serbian Radical Party. Now, the second person who is a member of the Serbian Radical Party, how do you know that he is such a member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I was in Nevesinje at the time when they were there, and he was recruiting people to join his party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were in that village, and he was encouraging people to join the Serbian Radical Party. This happened in 2007? We are talking about 2007; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nevesinje, is it located in Serbia or in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is located in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood correctly, in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 2007, the Serbian Radical Party had a political branch there where people were recruiting individuals to become members of the Serbian Radical Party, which was exercising political activities in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The recruitment was not in 2007. They started recruiting people from the end of the war, from 1996 onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question. Nevesinje, this village in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, is it located in the Republika Srpska or in the federation which currently exists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no questions for you. I shall ask my colleagues whether they have any questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. In your statements, you mention the arrival of JNA units in Mostar. You also mention the Green Berets. You mention a paratrooper regiment from Nis, the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to know whether at that time, which seems to be between June and July 1992, whether units of volunteers arrived also, groups of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you be a little bit more specific as regards these groups that arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That unit arrived. I cannot remember the exact date. I think it was the 6th of April, 1992. They came to Bjelusine. That is a neighbourhood in Mostar, Bjelusine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which group do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a group of some 50 or 60 men who came and introduced themselves as being from the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm a little bit ill. Now, this group comprising approximately 50 to 60 men was made up entirely of Serbs coming from Serbia or also of local Serbs, Bosnians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were local Serbs from Bosnia, too. I know that one introduced himself as a Bosnian from Vlasenica, I believe. However, they were immediately joined by some of the local Serbs from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Were there any other groups of volunteers different from the Seseljevci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I hadn't seen them, but there were these White Eagles. They said that they were stationed in Gacko. That's 40 or 50 kilometres away from Nevesinje. Then later on, in July 1992, a unit came. They were called Vukovarci, men from Vukovar. They had come from Croatia. I didn't have any information about these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to know precisely, Witness, whether you know anything about the co-operation between the White Eagles and the group Seselj's men.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that co-operation because this group that came from Mostar, that introduced themselves as Seseljevci, they were in Mostar, whereas this other group was in Bijelo Polje -- no, sorry, Gacko. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What distance is there from Mostar to Gacko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gacko is about 75 or 80 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, let's discuss some of the names you give in your statement. I would like to know who Relebic [as interpreted] was. According to you, he brought money back for his unit. You also add that the Serbian Radical Party always had money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for Radovic, he was commander of a special unit of the Army of Republika Srpska. They were called the Bjelica volunteers. Radovic, Rade Radovic. He went to Serbia, and whenever he'd come from Serbia he'd bring money for the needs of his troops. Now, where that money actually came from, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this was not a group of volunteers made up of Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were Seselj's men, but they were the Bjelica volunteers, and they, indeed, were members of the Serb Radical Party. However, these Bjelica volunteers were under the Army of Republika Srpska, whereas this first group that had come, consisting of 50 or 60 men that I'm talking about, they were not under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska. They had a relationship with the Yugoslav People's Army, and it's from the JNA that they received everything they needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Cvele, who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came from Serbia. He came to Mostar 25 or 30 years ago. And when they came to Bjelusine, he joined them. Cvele and Lika, that's what I know, that they joined them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give us the name of the group? Specify each time which group it is, whether you include the group of Seseljevci or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cvele and Lika, and a few other local Serbs, had joined this group that came to Mostar on the 6th of April, the first one. They said that they had been sent by Mr. Vojislav Seselj and that they were from the Serb Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this is something you heard those men tell you directly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. What were they supposed to tell me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said, if I had understood you correctly, that they were saying that they had been sent by Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something you heard from them directly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's now move on to the direct testimony you are giving us. Either you can deny or uphold this, i.e., crimes committed by some of the Seselj's men. Could you, first and foremost, tell us whether you were an eye-witness to this when these crimes were being committed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you expand on this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 13th of June, 1992, a sabotage group of the BH Army attacked, and we fought with them, and two or three men lost their lives. When we repelled that attack, we returned to Zalik about 6.30 in the evening, because our location was in Zalik. A woman came up to me and said that they had taken her son away, Nedzad Benca, that they took him away, and that he was somewhere in the changing rooms in Vrapcici. However, more and more people were coming there and saying that their husbands, children, et cetera, had been taken away. Then, Borislav Janjic and I went to look for these people. I actually went to look for this Nedzad Benca. When I came to the changing rooms, he was not there. However, there were quite a few people locked up there. Now, I don't know how many "quite a few" is, but there were really many of them. I was looking for Nedzad Benca, but a local person told me that they had already taken a group to Uborak, to a garbage dump there. Then this Bosanac, the Bosnian, came to me. He was from the Radical Party and he disarmed me and said, You want to protect the "balijas" here? Nobody is going to do that. Then Borislav and I quarreled with them a bit there, but a young man came up to us, and said, You'd better leave here. There's nothing here. Then we went to Uborak. When we got to Uborak, there were about 20 men there who had introduced themselves as being Seselj's men previously, and there were about 20 civilians. Among them were some local persons as well, among the Seseljevci; Diki Janjic, Mile Antelj. I can't remember who else was there. Then as we walked up to them, Mile Antelj -- I mean as we walked up to these people to see whether Benza was there, perhaps Mile Antelj said, You have no business here; go. We walked towards the car -- but Benca wasn't there. Before we entered the car -- as we were walking towards the car, they took them down into a valley, into a valley. We started towards the car, and they went in this other direction. When we got to the car, we heard shooting. We got into the car and fled. Afterwards, we heard that over 100 people had been killed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there's one thing I have not understood from your statements. If at some point in time you had been arrested, together with the Muslims and the Croats, by this group --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were arrested and detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they disarmed me. They took away my rifle, and they said that they would take me away and that I would end up like those people too. That's what Bosanac and Srecko -- that's what Bosanac said to me, and Bosanac was there with Srecko and other people I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few points of detail concerning Kandic. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean Zdravko Kandic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am talking about your statement of August 1998, where you say that 88 persons were purportedly killed, 30 of them in a forest, and the orders had come from Kandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that the order came from Kandic, the order to kill them. I said that Kandic had ordered to have these people detained, that he issued an order to have all these people brought together and detained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What about Savic; was he a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean Krsto Savic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about Miljenko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Miljenko Savic, yes, he was a military policeman at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say in that same statement that you were locked up in a cell and beaten by Miroslav Duka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was on the 5th of August, 1992, after all of these things that had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was Miroslav Duka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the chief of police in Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have a follow-up question for you after the questions put by Judge Lattanzi. As far as Mr. Seselj's men are concerned, in your statement of 1998 you mention a number of names which I shall remind you of. You say that there was Rasko Janjic, nicknamed Diki; Damir Antelj, Borislav Miskin, Ses Pejak, Slavko Milovanovic, Dragan Antelj, Miroslav Antelj, Mile Antelj, Slobodan Umicevic, Novica Antelj, and Boskajlo Kovacevic, so you mention the names of a number of individuals who, in 1992, were Seselj's men. You say this in 1998; i.e., six years later. I apologise. My memory doesn't operate the same way as yours does. I would be totally unable to give you the names of those witnesses I have examined, even though I may have spent a number of days with these witnesses. Therefore, do you have a remarkable memory to such an extent that you are able to give the names of eight people who, according to you, belong to Seselj? How are you able to do this? I apologise. How are you able to remember eight names like this, those eight names you gave the investigator; because you have a remarkable memory, quite unique?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, sir, but the people that I enumerated, and I never said they were Seselj's men. They were the local population. They were the local population. They were there with them, but they weren't Seselj's men. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen carefully. This is what is written in your statement, in the English version: You say that they were a number of Seselj's men: "The ones I knew were ...," and then you mention them, give their names. Are you giving names of locals or Seselj's men? Because when you read this -- when the sentence is read, the impression you get is that the names you mention are Seselj's men. Or are these locals who belonged to different groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, they were local men. I knew them. I knew their full names, and they were from Mostar. Now, the others, the Seselj men who came, from Serbia, and they just had nicknames. None of them introduced themselves by giving their first and last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Seselj's men who came from Serbia only had nicknames. This is clear. One last question. This is from paragraph 27 of your 2004 statement. This is probably the most important paragraph in the entire statement. This is what you say: "Seselj and his political party was almost unknown in Mostar because there was no SRS party headquarter in Mostar." And you add: "The first such office of the SRS was established in Bjelica at the beginning of the war." And you add: "I also observed that an SRS office had been established in Nevesinje." And you go on: "The first SRS officer in Bjelica was Ljubo Kapor, who was a vojvoda, but he was killed in August 1992." Then you say that the other local SRS leader was Rade Radovic, who later also became a vojvoda, and that in 1991 this group had participated in the attack of Dubrovnik from Trebinje, and the soldiers were still members of the SRS with proper membership cards. This is what you are saying on paragraph 27. How did you know that Ljubo Kapor and Rade Radovic were members of the SRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we know that because Mr. Seselj, in 1994, went to see Rade Radovic in Nevesinje at their positions there, and they openly said that they were -- well, Rade Radovic would always say that he was going to Serbia, to the Serbian Radical Party somewhere, and that they gave him assistance in the form of food, money, clothing, footwear, everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're saying that Mr. Seselj came to Nevesinje in 1994 and he met Rade Radovic there. So according to you, Rade Radovic was a member of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, obviously, I assume so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You assume so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I apologise, but I need you to give us some additional information. I had asked you whether, among Seselj's men, there were also locals, and you answered by saying that there were also locals and not just Serbs from Serbia; there were also Serbs from Bosnia. So if I understood you correctly when answering a question put to you by the Presiding Judge, you said that Seselj's men were not locals, they came from Serbia. So maybe I misunderstood you, but I detect a contradiction here. So could you shed some light on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Local people. When I say "local people," I mean the people who originate from the area, for example, from Mostar. They were joined by two, three, maybe five - I'm not quite sure of the number - these from Vlasenica. Vlasenica is in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We didn't consider them to be locals. Vlasenica is in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so they weren't considered the local population, because I never actually saw those people. So Vlasenica is about 300 kilometres away from Mostar, 250 to 300 kilometres, so I can't call them locals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understand now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question, and then I will give the floor to my fellow Judge. Are you really saying the following: Among Seselj's men, some came from Serbia? This is what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, most of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say most of them, they were in the majority. Now, those who came from Serbia, could you give us a figure? Could we know how many there were, a ballpark figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 55 to 60 people in three trucks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fifty-five to sixty in three trucks. When they arrived, did they have weapons, uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A leader?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had uniforms and everything they needed. They had weapons, rifles, everything they needed. They would get them from the JNA. They would go to the main command, the headquarters of the JNA, and get them there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you see, when we put questions, we obtain very important details. Seselj's men, who numbered 55 to 60, came on board three trucks, but they had obtained weapons and uniforms at the JNA. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we saw them when they arrived. They parked in front of the school in Bjelusine. They got out. They were all wearing camouflage uniforms and bearing weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question. You told us you saw these men. They arrived in front of the school. According to you, did they report to the JNA, were they under JNA command; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't say, because they arrived and told us that they were Serbian Radicals, and some of them even had some booklets of the Serbian Radical Party. They said that they had every possibility to procure whatever we needed from the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, just to clarify one small point that came out of the questions that were put to you by my two colleagues at the Bench. When the three trucks arrived with Seselj's men to Mostar, you said that they were equipped by the JNA, yet you also said that when they got out of the trucks, they already had camouflage uniforms and their weapons with them before they entered the JNA headquarters in Mostar. I'm not quite sure of what your testimony really is, so let me put a question to you to clarify this. Were they already dressed in camouflage uniforms and armed with rifles when they came in the trucks, or did they only get their uniforms and their weapons once they had entered the JNA headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came armed and had camouflage uniforms on them. That's how they came. And the JNA barracks was about a kilometre away from Bjelusine, and they would go every day brining back weapons and whatever they needed. They had everything. We didn't even have cigarettes. They had everything. Where they got it all from, who supplied them, I have no idea. However, when they arrived in Mostar, they had -- when they got off the trucks, they had rifles and uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. So what exactly did they get from the JNA? If they brought already their own weapons and had everything they needed, what could they possibly get from the JNA in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they would get ammunition, food - what do you call them? - those RPGs, hand-held rocket-launchers, the Zolja type. They just came with light weapons. Everything else they got from the JNA; anti-tank mines, mines for the destruction of tanks and things like that, launchers and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very useful information. Now, during the events that you have described in your statements to the Prosecution, you mentioned that there were, of course, the JNA, who had their headquarters in the barracks. You also mentioned a number of paramilitary groups, one of which were Seselj's men, and you also mentioned the TO. My question is if you were able to form an impression about how the activities of these three groups were co-ordinated during the events which you describe in your statements. My question is, really: Were these groups acting more or less individually or was it your impression that they were under an overall central command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think, quite simply, they were under an overall central command, under the JNA, because they would all address the JNA. Anything they needed, they procured from the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army. For example, if you wanted to leave Mostar, you needed a permit to be signed personally by Momcilo Perisic. I was never able to get a permit like that. But these volunteers coming in from Serbia, whenever they wanted to and needed to, and they could even sign those permits themselves, come to that. Where they got the permits from, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. But when it came to the operations that you have described, was it your impression that these operations had been planned and ordered and initiated by the central command of the JNA, or was it operations that were planned and carried out individually by those groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was planned and carried out individually by those groups. I'm not quite sure. I don't really know, but that's my opinion, because they didn't have to tell anybody what they were doing. They looted and so on. They weren't held accountable. There was no law or order there for a month while the Serbs were there. There was no police, nothing. It was total chaos and anarchy, lawlessness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, you have described that very convincingly in your statements. Just to follow up on this point, in the actions that took place that you have described, the looting and the operations, was there anyone present from the JNA who could actually oversee and perhaps control the actions? Was there anyone present to represent the overall command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, General Momcilo Perisic. For example, from Mostar to Nevesinje, there were six to seven check-points along the way, and you had to show your permit or authorisation at each of those check-points, and that permit can only be signed by Momcilo Perisic. So somebody had to oversee it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. But, of course, Momcilo Perisic could not possibly have been present at all those six to seven check-points, nor could he have been present at the actions and the events which you describe in your statements, so my question is really: Was there some JNA officer present along with the paramilitary groups during the events which you describe in your statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never saw an officer with any paramilitary group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So when the paramilitary groups acted in Mostar and in Nevesinje, they acted on their own, without there being any officer from the JNA present; is that a correct version of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now, you say that you were part of the TO. Could you tell us who was the commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My superior was Rade Markovic, and his superior was Zdravko Kandic in North Camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who did Zdravko Kandic report to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the superior to everybody was General Momcilo Perisic. Now, who was his immediate superior, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I was very impressed by the answer you gave to my fellow Judge. You said that it was chaos. Now, we can imagine that. But you also said that in order to move around, there were check-points, that it was impossible -- and you could only move around if General Perisic had authorised this trip. So on the one hand, there's chaos, but on the other hand, there's also control. So was it organised chaos or was it that General Perisic was completely incompetent and only able to place check-points on the roads and leave all the rest to pretty much anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems that that's how it was, sir, because if you had to go from Mostar to Nevesinje, which is 37 kilometres, there were six or seven check-points, and at each check-point you were asked for your papers, authorisation to exit town. But when you come into town, nobody asked you anything anymore. Total chaos prevailed; killings, abuse, mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, outside Mostar General Perisic was in control of the situation, but within the city it was chaos.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question, and then we will have a break, and then the Prosecutor will start his cross-examination. So one last question before the break. You told us that the people who came from Serbia would arrive in this JNA barracks, where they were provided with heavy equipment, and then in passing you said that they had brought their own light weapons. If I understand you correctly - I'm trying to imagine all this and understand what happened - the Serbian volunteers would leave Serbia with their own weapons, light weapons, of course - they didn't have any tanks or RPGs or rocket-launchers, but they had their own light weapons - they would arrive to the barracks, where they were provided with a uniform, where they were equipped? Is this what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came in camouflage uniforms and light weapons, but everything else they needed they got from the JNA. They would go to North Camp or South Camp, and from there they would obtain everything they needed, from cigarettes, food, rocket-launchers, the lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was right to put this question to you, because you just said that they arrived in uniforms with light weapons. Does this mean that before they arrived to the JNA barracks, where they were provided with the rest of the equipment, they had already been through a JNA barracks where they were provided with uniforms and weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't say, because I only saw them when they arrived, the moment they arrived. Where they were before that, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is a very precise answer. You are telling us exactly what you saw, i.e., that they already had uniforms and light weapons, and in those JNA barracks they obtained heavy weaponry, but you cannot say where they obtained their equipment earlier. This is very precise. It is now time for our break. We will break, and then the Prosecutor will have one hour for his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a brief objection before Mr. Marcussen starts. During the break, I asked the Registrar to ask the Prosecutor to make available to me my book, "Podgoricki Atentat," "The Assassination in Podgorica." While I was meeting my disclosure obligations in advance, I gave it to the OTP six years ago. I wanted to use the book. However, the OTP refused to help me out, and they don't want to make this book available to me. I am convinced that it is their duty to make it available at any point when it may be needed, because that is the point of disclosure, to have the book used in the proceedings. Therefore, I ask you now to order the Prosecution to make this book available to me during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, what about this book? From what I understand, Mr. Seselj has seemingly given this book six years ago to the OTP, and he would like to have his book back. Why don't you want to give him his book back?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a small correction. I don't want the book back. I just want to use it for one minute here, and I'll return it to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, he would just like to have a look at his book for one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was apprised of this request probably three minutes ago. The accused has just told us now on the fly that he wants to use the book. We probably have it somewhere, if we can find it. It is the accused's duty to prepare his cross-examination, to come with the documents that he intends to use. It is not for the Prosecution to bring documents to court that he would like to use in court. Now, secondly, if he's going to use the book for the purpose of his cross-examination, what copy is the Prosecution going to have so that we can follow what he's using in cross-examination of the witness? I respectfully submit that the accused needs to prepare his own cross-examination and come with the documents that he needs. Now, if I'm directed to provide the book, we will go and see if we can find it somewhere. I don't know if it's in our vault or standing on a shelf somewhere, but if the Chamber would like us to, we will undertake to try to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm convinced that you going to do your utmost, since you are a great professional, and this is why I believe there might be a misunderstanding. You said, If I give the book, how will I be able to use it if I don't have it? Mr. Seselj told us that he only wants to look at it for a minute, and then he will give it back to you. So there's no problem there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The way the accused normally deals with these extensive documents that he reads out from this, that he puts propositions to the witnesses from various documents. When he does that with a document in a language where we don't have a translation, I'm having the assistance of somebody who understands the language, so I can see whether or not the propositions that are being put are correct. I cannot do that if I don't have a copy of the material that the accused is using. That's my point. I, of course, trust that the accused would give us back the book. I have no worry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, then. You may start. Mr. Marcussen, try and find this book again, give it to him over the break. He will have 20 minutes to look at it, and he will give you the book back once he starts his questions. So you may begin with your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one point, Mr. President. On the basis of the questions put by you, the Judges, I realised that I might find the book useful. Otherwise, I did not think that I'd need the book. That can happen in any trial. What is handed over to the Prosecution has to be available all the time. It cannot simply be lost. I didn't give it to them for fun. I gave it to them by way of disclosure, material for them to familiarise themselves with. They've had six years to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I have a problem with this procedure. According to our procedure, you are the one who selects the documents you wish to use during your cross-examination. You have the documents translated into English or into French so that the Trial Chamber may use these documents also; in English so that the Prosecutor may follow. This is what poses a problem. I understand now you would like him to give this to you so that you can use it, and it is in Serbian, so we would not be able to understand it. It will only be for you to refresh your memory relating to what this document contains, but it is not for the Prosecutor or for the Trial Chamber to be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Lattanzi, according to Rule 65 ter it is my duty to disclose on time -- disclosure related to my case, just like the OTP has the duty to disclose their material to me. It is all of six years ago that I disclosed to them all of my books, 80 books, and the first editions, at that, so that they would be as authentic as possible and as contemporaneous as possible, in view of the charges in the indictment. If I disclosed it to the Prosecution, they cannot simply say, Well, we'll see if we find it, because the Prosecutor has to find this at any point in time. They are an officer of international justice here. They should be interested in international justice and the truth. It's not a question of succeeding at all costs. Here, there is a difference between the Prosecution and the accused person in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stress the point. You are the one who needs to ask for the translation of portions of this book. It's not a matter of a thousand pages. These are just the portions which are relevant to you, to defend your case, and you select these passages and you have them translated, and you then disclose them to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I did not refer to the problem of translation here at all, just the problem of making the book available for one minute; nothing more than that. The book does not have to be translated. It is the Prosecutor who is complicating things now. They refuse to co-operate. The Prosecutor always has to co-operate with the Defence. They have to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Maybe the Prosecution is unable, at three minutes' notice, to find the book, because as you are probably aware, the stock of evidence that is contained by the Prosecution is enormous and it may not be possible, in three minutes, to produce your book. But as I understand, the Prosecution will find the book and you will have it for the next break. May I suggest we simply stop this and move on. Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not insist to have it done within three minutes' time. I did not insist on three minutes. I was thinking of at least one hour or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, you are going to make sure you find this book and give it to the accused during the break. We have wasted ten minutes for a one-minute issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: VS-1067, I'd like to go back over some of the issues that have already been covered, in part, but to try to cover in a chronological fashion some of the things that have already been talked about today. Let me just ask you, first of all, if you could describe to the Judges the ethnic composition of the population living on the east and the west side of the Neretva River, in Mostar? Who lived on the west side and the east side, in majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean before the war or during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Before the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think 42 per cent were Muslims, 30 per cent Serbs, and about 30 per cent Croats. I don't know exactly. Before the war, the town was not divided into the left and right bank. It was a single city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were there a majority of one ethnic group on one side and of another group on the other side, or were everyone mixed up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were all mixed. In the villages around Mostar, it was different. Say Rastani, 70 per cent Serb; Bijelo Polje, 60 or 70 per cent Serb; Vrapcici, something like that, too; Orlic, Serbs. Then up there in the mountains, there were Muslims. Here on the other side, on the right-hand side there were Croats. And in town, they were all mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In Mostar, were there any military camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was the northern and the southern camp. Two barracks, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was there a military airport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A military airport was to the south of Mostar, about seven or eight kilometres south. I didn't count that as a military camp. I don't know how to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When did -- was that airport always a military airport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was a military airport, but I think -- I think, I say, I think that even civilian aircraft landed there. But it was used for military purposes the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You say in your 1998 statement that it was a civilian airport, but that the army took it over in 1992. Does that reflect your recollection or do you think -- are you unsure about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, it's been 18 years. I can't remember whether it was a civilian or a military airport. I know that civilian aeroplanes landed there. For example, when the football club went to play matches elsewhere, their planes would take off from there, so it means that it was used for civilian purposes too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did there come a time when roadblocks started to be set up in the Mostar area, the Mostar-Nevesinje area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mostar-Nevesinje, Mostar-Sarajevo. There were barricades in Salakovac, held by the Serbs, and up by Grebak, also roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, pass through those roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was going from Sarajevo to Mostar, there was the roadblock in Salakovac. They -- the Serbs won't let me go by, and I had to go up Prozor and Kupres in order to get to Mostar. I was about 12 kilometres away from Mostar, but I had to take a 250-kilometre road in order to get home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was there a roadblock put up in Nevesinje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a roadblock -- I mean from Mostar to Nevesinje, if that's what you mean, when the war started, there were five or six roadblocks held by the Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know who was the leader or the commander of those who were manning those roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the JNA all the way up to Podvelezje. And at Grebak, the Chetniks of Arsen Grahovac, they said they held check-points there. They were the local Serbs from Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were they a member of any particular organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Arsen Grahovac's men were the Serb Chetnik Movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was the Serb Chetnik Movement established in Nevesinje? Did they have a branch there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know when it was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when it was established. But even before the war, in 1991, I heard that the Chetnik Movement of Karadjordje or something like that was founded, and this Arsen Grahovac was their commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, I should just explain to you I'm sort of moving back and forth and turning on and off my microphone. It's not to be impolite, but it's to make the security measures work properly. Now, do you know how many men were under Grahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 150 men. That's what they said. However, I don't know. They said that there were about 150 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: At some point, were there JNA reservists coming to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They came in September 1991, and between 20.000 and 30.000 of them came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know where they came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: At some point, was there a call for mobilisation or mobilisation orders issued in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mid-September, then perhaps started in mid-October. I can't remember exactly, but I know that people received call-up papers for mobilisation. There was only Serbs who were mobilised. As for Muslims, if they came for mobilisation, they said, Well, if necessary, we are going to call you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were others who reported for mobilisation, but they didn't want to give them rifles and things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did there come a point when the Croats declared Mostar the capital of the Croatian Community in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1991, they declared Mostar the Croatian capital, that it would be the capital of Herceg-Bosna. That's what that man used to say. Now, what was his name? Jadranko Prlic, whatever. I can't remember what his name was, the name of this gentleman who was making these statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like it to be recorded that I cannot put any questions because I am sitting on a trial in the case of Jadranko Prlic, so I will not put any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In November/December, did the atmosphere start to change in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These reservists who came from Montenegro, they were drinking, shooting. They started mistreating everyone, regardless of whether they were Serbs, Croats, Muslims. They disturbed everyone, regardless of what faith people belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And just in the interest of time, do I understand correctly that there came a point in time when you and your family were expelled from your houses by Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They came to the door of my house, and they asked for my rifle. I fled. My mother and my two brothers were expelled. And I fled through the window, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And was that -- am I correct that was on the 6th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, when the barracks -- well, when the barracks went down. It was three days or so later, the 6th of April. You have to understand that they expelled 25.000 to 30.000 Serbs from the Neretva River Valley, and it wasn't that they were only maltreating me, but others as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And after this, was there any action by the JNA towards Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they shelled Mostar every day, every day, from the Northern Camp, the Southern Camp, the airport, from Fortica, Hum, the hills around Mostar. There was shooting non-stop. However, at first, at the beginning of April, when they started targeting the city, Perisic said over the radio -- he announced that he would target such and such a locality and that the civilians should seek shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And am I correct that this is the same time that you testified earlier today, that the volunteer group of Seselj's men came on two or three trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you told who the leader of that group was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the Seselj group?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of them said he was Mico Drazic or that he was the leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a person called Slobodan Zubak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slobodan Zubac, not Zubak with a K; with a C. Slobodan Zubac was the leader of the local Serbs in Bjelusine. Yes, I am familiar with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you remember if there were any contacts between the group of SRS volunteers that arrived in Mostar and him, that is, Zubac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Can you explain what contacts there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What contacts there were, I don't know. But I know that they were in his house, and they -- and in Slobodan Zubac's house weapons were being distributed to Serbs coming from Mostar on one occasion. And they went to his house, they would discuss matters, so they had contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you see this yourself, the weapons and the discussions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And was this around this time, the 6th or 7th of April, or at another time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was sometime in April, because I was in Bjelusine in April. I don't know until when. (redacted) (redacted). I also saw at his place there was just light weapons, rifles and bombs or hand-grenades. He didn't have any heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Just to clarify, when you say weapons were being distributed, were they also distributed to the members of Seselj's men, to some of the people who had come on those trucks, or were they distributed to someone else, the weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was weapons distributed to people -- Serbs coming from Mostar, who came in and joined up with the Territorial Defence. It wasn't still the army at the time, the Army of Republika Srpska. It was the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. In your -- are you familiar with a location called Copla [sic]?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Topla, Topla. It's a place about one to one and a half kilometres away from Bjelusine towards Fortica and towards Podvelezje, inhabited by purely Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how big is that location? How many houses, for example, or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps 30 to 40 houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you see any members of the SRS there ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw members of the SRS when they brought out television sets, washing machines, white goods generally, cars that had been abandoned. They drove the cars and loaded up the white goods onto trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of the people involved in this looting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was this man Mico Drazic, then some man called Vranjanac and Srecko. There was some 10 or 15. I can't remember them all. I know there was Vranjanac, Srecko, Mico Drazic. Mico Drazic once drove off a full truck-load from this village of Topla with white goods. He drove off towards Nevesinje. What happened later on, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Generally, what was the attitude of the local population -- the local Serb population towards the SRS volunteers and the group you described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, people were afraid of them. They were afraid of them because they even killed each other. There was certain cases where they killed their own members. They were quite wild, so people were afraid of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to talk a bit about some of the groups that already have been discussed today, but other groups than the SRS group that we just talked about. First, could I ask you, are you familiar with something called the 63rd Parachute Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know where that came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were from Nis, and the unit was called the Mungos, and they were stationed in Rastani. Mungos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And just so we know, Nis, what republic is that and where is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbia, and I think it said "63rd Parachute Division." They had some insignia to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What did they look like, the insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't really remember. I know that there was a parachute and a mouse or something, and then it said "Mungos" underneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you see them involved in any sniping activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had snipers. Now, whether they -- well, they shot from Razvitak, but you couldn't see them when they went into a building. But they had snipers, they had noise dampers, silencers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Who were they shooting at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were shooting on the right-hand side. Whether they were shooting at civilians or the army, I really can't say. I didn't see exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a union called the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What kind of a unit was that; police, military, volunteers? What were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a military unit, and the commander was Dragan Zirojevic, nicknamed Zira, and Baca Milosevic, and what was the other man's name? I can't remember. There was another man name, but I can't remember his name now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I think we've managed to produce a nice hot, warm copy of the book that the accused has requested, so I'd like to hand it over so he can look for what he wants to look for. And since it's a copy, I'm informed that the accused can keep his copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the Nevesinje Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Who was the commander of that brigade, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander was -- I think in February 1994, it was Novica Gusic, and after him Zoran Purkovic took over. I can't remember the exact date, but I know that Novica Gusic was the first commander. He's from Nevesinje otherwise, but he personally boasted and said that he was in Vukovar and that for his merits he was given the command of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we can now talk about May 1992, and more specifically the 12th of May. Were you in an operation that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was coming from the direction of Brankovci, and then we went down to the National Theatre, and there we came across Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let me just stop you. Were you in Capljina that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not that day, we weren't in Capljina -- I wasn't in Capljina, no. Capljina is 55 kilometres away from Mostar, and that's where the hotbed of the Croatian Army was. There was just a barracks there. And from Mostar, they would target Capljina from the airport to pull out the soldiers from the barracks. They used helicopters and I don't know what else, and they managed to pull the soldiers up from -- out from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let's get back, then, to the incident I think you started to describe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, the witness told us that he was coming from the direction of Brankovci, and then he goes on to say that, We went down to the National Theatre, and there we came across Muslims and Croats. My question is: Who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Who are "we"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were going from -- well, it's an inhabited area, so we moved forward going from house to house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what were your orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To liberate the left bank of the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And who had given you those orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was personally given the order from -- well, to our unit, Major Ugresic, who was in North Camp. It was an order from the JNA, and he was a JNA colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you describe to us what you saw when you came to the National Theatre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, nothing. When we reached the National Theatre, there was a bit of resistance there, but we managed to break through them, and we pushed them back to the left bank. And the soldiers passed by first, and then after us came Seselj's men. We didn't touch the civilians or anything. But they looted and so on. As far as they were concerned, what their eyes saw, their hands took. They took everything. They just stole and looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Why do you say these people were Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because that's how they introduced themselves, and they had some membership booklets of the Serbian Radical Party. And I was up at the check-points by Nevesinje when they were stopped. They were stopped by Krsto Savic, and Krsto Savic was the commander -- police commander for Herzegovina, for the whole area of Herzegovina, and people asked him, Who are these? And he said, Seselj's men. And they also showed some documents to him. He would examine them. I have no idea what they were. But, anyway, that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was that on the 12th of May or was it another day that they were stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in May, up in Nevesinje. It was another day, not that day, while I was waiting for a truck from Mostar or to Mostar. They would be stopped at a check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So would it be correct to summarise what you said, that you recognised these men as being the same ones that you then saw again on the 12th, behind the lines that you were in when you were in Mostar on the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did Seselj's men take anyone into the National Theatre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did, the Croat. And when I saw this Croat, he was all -- well, his face was completely distorted from the beatings. And then later on they took him away and mistreated him in the National Theatre and took him down to Bunur, an area as you're going to the old town. And then they threw him into a shaft and threw two hand-grenades in the shaft and killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How do you know that they threw him into the shaft and threw grenades in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on, when the people cleared the area, there was a stench. You can imagine what stench there is coming from a corpse when the temperature is 35 degrees. You couldn't get within several hundred metres of the area from the stench.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How do you know that it was Seselj's men and not someone else who threw him into the shaft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they took him away. They took him there. And that shaft was at a distance from the National Theatre of some 50 to 70 metres. It's just one street between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In May of 1992, did you see any human bodies in Mostar, in Eastern Mostar, lying in the streets perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were some. If you went down Tito Street, there were corpses on all sides, and that was mid-May. There were people killed. They were lying 'round about on the road. I don't know who collected up the bodies later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you described this in your statement, but it's not clear. And what I wanted to clarify is: Were these bodies civilians or military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you able to identify the ethnicity of any of these people or can you not tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Who were in control of that part of Mostar at this particular point in time in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that part in Mostar was controlled by the Serbs. However, that part wasn't actually controlled by anybody, because there was general lawlessness, chaos, and anarchy. You could lose your head in a second. If you weren't with them or if you just happened to say something that somebody didn't like, you could be killed. Nobody was answered -- was held accountable for anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, moving to the events on June 13th, 1992, that you already described or testified about, I'd like to ask you about the beginning of those events. You were given an order to participate in an operation. What was your order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what operation you mean. Do you mean when we were fighting against the Muslims and Croats in battle or when Mr. Kandic ordered something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry. Kandic's order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kandic ordered us -- well, he -- that was around 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon. We were fighting the Croats and Muslims. A sabotage group was infiltrated, and when we dealt with them -- when we finished our business with them, then Kandic said -- or somebody came and said that Kandic had ordered all the civilians to be collected up for interrogation because those civilians were possibly hiding the saboteurs in their houses or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the collected civilians, where were they to be taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were to be taken to North Camp, that's where they were supposed to be taken, but we didn't take them anywhere. My group didn't take them anywhere because we knew all those local people. They were all locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But I understood from your evidence today that other units must have taken people to these places. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, other units did take people off. They took them to the football stadium at Vrapci and the dressing rooms there or changing rooms. May I have five minutes to go to the toilet, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can go ahead. We'll wait. Go ahead. Usher, could you please escort the witness, and then we'll wait for his return. Just a minute. We need to drop the blinds first. In order to save time, we'll break right now, and then we will resume at 12.00, and we'll continue non-stop until 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I continue my examination of the witness, I wondered whether the accused, now that he has had the break to look at his book, could indicate to us what pages from this rather voluminous book that he intends to refer the witness to when we get to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I haven't found the page, but it is easy to find. Oh, my microphone wasn't on. It's on now. Mr. Marcussen's associate can help him. Benis [as interpreted] was in Podgorica on the 25th of May with me and that he was wounded there, and I referred to this several times during the examination of some other witnesses. And I'd like to raise that; nothing more. And as far as Miroslav Vukovic, Cele, is concerned, he was also wounded in Podgorica. Forty-two pieces of shrapnel from the bomb were found in his body, and this case was tried in Podgorica, the assassin case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, from what I have understood, the date of the 25th of May, 1992, is mentioned in the book, the arrival of Mr. Seselj, together with Olivia Barret [as interpreted], B-a-r-r-e-t, as well as Miroslav Vukovic, who seemingly was wounded. That's it. Well, we will see things a bit better later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We have been given no assistance by the accused. I am not able to understand in Cyrillic how to find this. Now, the other thing is during the break the accused has provided some documents that he's going to use for cross-examination. From my very limited understanding of this, or, rather, the briefing that I have been given, my impression is that some of the documents concern an issue that might have been unexpected and that came up today in response to one of the Judges' question, but one of the documents is a document regarding a Radovic who has been discussed here a number of times. Now, Radovic is also referred to in the statements of the witness's, and therefore there's no reason that the accused could not have provided this document earlier. It has been clear all the time that the witness would be giving this evidence, and we should have been provided this and the Court should have been provided this at the beginning of the witness testimony. So I object to the accused's use of this particular document which has been provided to us during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, in the witness's statement made under oath, Radovic is a member, according to him, of the Serbian Radical Party. This is what I have understood. The documents in Cyrillic, which I don't know anything about, may indicate that he belongs to another party. Let's wait and see what questions are put during the cross-examination, and then you may put further questions after that. For the moment, I have no information, but in light of the case file I have some idea of what might happen afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, but this illustrates the problem. The document is not translated, is provided last minute. Now, I'm able to assist the Court by providing you the information that this is apparently some sort of membership registration for this particular person, and that's what I'm saying. This could have been brought to everyone's attention much earlier than during the break. We only got it at noon. I guess Your Honours also just received it now. So I'm objecting to the use of that document. The other documents which have to do with elections, I'm not objecting to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I really thought that I'd refrain from any further objections so that we would finish with this witness today. However, that will not be possible, obviously. This is the first time I hear today that Dragan Samardzic and Drago Tamindzija are my associates. Today is the first time I hear of this. No one ever said that to me before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm not objecting to the election documents. I'm objecting to use of the registration of Radovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed. We'll see this later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the sixth document, I don't have to use it at all. This is just Radovan Radovic's application form dated the 15th of October, 1994, when joining the Serb Radical Party. Radovan Radovic was mentioned several times, including last week by Dabic. However, no war crimes are linked to Radovan Radovic. There is no reason for me to prove when he became a member of the party. They sent me this just like that, along with other documents.
