utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But as I have heard, they were well known in Mostar as drug addicts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zurovac and Edo or Edin Ramadanovic, they never took drugs, and I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What about this Boris Kozul?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the leader of the Velez supporters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did you socialise in some cafe called Garden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Garden, let me see. Well, we did go 'round the cafes. I can't say for sure. Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then there was some Black Label Cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I never went in there. My foot never set foot in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But Sasa Zurovac was accused of looting that cafe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that could very well be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He didn't want to uncover his associates in front of the -- before the court, so he took the whole blame upon himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How don't you know? He was your friend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you know that person had committed various crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I would be proud of a friend of mine who took all the blame upon himself and didn't want to implicate others, but very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could that be redacted, please? Could we have that name redacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. We're not going to mention it, then. I don't want to say anything -- it's not in my interest to say anything in private session, so we'll skip that. There were a number of incidents with the reservists in Mostar; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what about Croats; did they plant bombs and throw hand-grenades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cafe Azaro, Cafe Gringo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So there was a lot of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the eve of celebrations and holidays. I can't remember all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. And some people, and we saw that from the article, accuse you of using marijuana?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Can I interrupt you there? I smoked hashish for the first time in 1997 here in Holland.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it's legal here. It's been legalised; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Some people accused you of having a whole marijuana plantation in Zijemlje in front of Cira's weekend cottage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but that's not true. Marijuana won't grow at a high altitude in the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, what's the altitude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see. Very well. That's what some people say about you. And when I collected this information, I didn't tell them what I needed the information for. Do you believe me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Let's see what's next. You mentioned here the crime in Zalik, linked to Vrapcici and Zijemlje, and it is a unique crime -- or it's one crime, although the killings took part in two parts, and everything happened when the JNA left Mostar; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And it was a spontaneous retaliation for -- revenge for crimes committed on the opposite side to the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what kind of revenge, who issued the orders. I really can't say. I don't know. Why those people were killed, I really can't tell you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you didn't see any of the killings personally; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the people manning the check-point, they were all military policemen, except at the entrance to Nevesinje; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And those who held the check-point in Nevesinje, you tied them to Arsen Grahovac, linked them to Arsen Grahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So they have nothing to do with the volunteers that I could have sent in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I'm going to complete my examination within the prescribed time, you can rest assured. I haven't got much longer to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned this Radovan Radovic's unit, and you first of all mentioned this man Kapor who was killed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Kapor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How do you know that Ljubo Kapor was a member of the Serbian Radical Party at all? Where do you get that from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the volunteers from Bjelica told me that, and that he was a vojvoda. Now, who could have given him that title, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of vojvoda he could have been. Now, do you know that I proclaimed the first Serbian Chetnik vojvodas only in May 1993? You don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the basis of my information, in Bjelica there was no branch of the Serbian Radical Party in 1992, and Radovan Radovic joined up with the Serbian Radical Party in 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says here the 15th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I promised the Prosecutor that I wasn't going to refer to the document, but I have my own information. I know when he became a member. But you, sir, were a member -- were there to see him in August 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did go to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But he didn't become a member straight away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that. Well, I visited various front-lines. Why wouldn't I have visited him?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What about Cicciolina? Why didn't you visit Cicciolina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't want to go to Cicciolina, establish inter-party relations with some Italian politicians at the time. Perhaps later on, I might have done so, but not linked to Rade Radovic and the others. They did not commit any crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I know that the summer I visited them, I prevailed upon Radovan Radovic -- I tried to persuade him to become a member of the Serbian Radical Party. And I managed to convince him and he did become a member, and you saw when he became a member. And I proclaimed him a Serbian Chetnik vojvoda on the occasion, because I did not want to have any Serbian Chetnik vojvodas proclaimed, anybody who is not a member of the Serbian Radical Party, in view of the fact that we had the Serbian Chetnik Movement as a component part of the Serbian Radical Party, which does not include the existence of various other Chetnik organisations that had nothing to do with us. I suppose that's clear to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that to this day in Republika Srpska, there are some Chetnik organisations that have nothing to do with the Serb Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, around Brcko. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In various places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Herzegovina too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that in Serbia there are Chetnik organisations that have nothing to do with the Serb Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can the Serb Radical Party, that is proud of its Chetnik traditions, can it have a monopoly on these traditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You stated one more thing here, that the Serb Radical Party from Belgrade assisted Radovan Radovic and his unit both financially and in equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what he said to us. Before we went into action, because the Bjelica volunteers in Cicciolina went into action together, two or three days before every action he went to Belgrade and he brought uniforms, food, cigarettes, everything from Belgrade. And he, himself, Rade Radovic, said that he got money from the Serb Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm interested in how come that money was there and they didn't really have that much money. We primarily provided them with cigarettes and canned food.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what they brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I visited them twice in 1994 and 1995. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know about 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In 1994, he hadn't joined the party yet, and by 1995 he was already a member of the Serb Radical Party and a Chetnik vojvoda. What I could do then was to give them a gift of 1.000 Deutchemark so that they can treat themselves to a crate of beer and things like that. Can you believe that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they have any kind of big money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, I could not say that they really had any kind of big money. They did have a bit more than us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could these have been voluntary contributions for a unit that became famous, and then somebody would give 50 and somebody would give 100 or 200 Deutchemark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can your statement be reduced to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of cigarettes we could have and send to our volunteers at the front-line? Did you ever see those cigarettes when we would send them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw them. We smoked those cigarettes. I can't remember what brand they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were they originally packed or were they there on a wholesale basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Wholesale, in large quantities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So then you can confirm that we got, as a gift from the tobacco factory in Bjelusine, all the cigarettes that the machine would throw out during manufacturing? They're proper cigarettes, but then some of them simply get thrown out during the manufacturing process, and then they collected them for us and put them in these big carton boxes for us. Did you see such box?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there were 200 or 300 cigarettes per box.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were even more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's what they brought to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then we handed out these boxes to our volunteers so that smokers could have cigarettes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it wasn't any kind of luxury cigarettes, not in the original packing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It is what we barely managed to get our hands on. What about food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cans, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And sometimes a sack of flour, beans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What could we send by way of clothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How did we get uniforms in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. They always had new uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They had new uniforms because they were an elite unit consisting of very brave fighters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, but I was there too, and I went with that unit to all the front-lines in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that in 1994 and 1995, we had severely clashed with Milosevic's regime and we simply could not get anything from state warehouses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So where could we get any uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nowhere, but they did have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But they did not get them from the Army of Republika Srpska? Did they have some kind of priority or a factory manufactured had manufactured more and gave it to them as a gift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is possible, but they didn't have more priority than we did from the Army Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you think of a factory of this kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a factory in Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the factory from Bjelica manufacture that for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You could have known?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If the factory in Bjelica manufactured uniforms, and if they have that detachment from Bjelica that became famous at many front-lines --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: -- what would be more natural than that? Now, why am I insisting on this? Because the Prosecution claims in the indictment as well that the Serb Radical Party financed volunteers. The Serb Radical Party could not have financed anyone, and I assert that. Am I right when I say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If I'm not right, the question arises straight away as to where we got our money.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for financing, they did get cigarettes and tinned food for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Seselj, I do not think that this witness is in a position to testify as to where the SRS got its money from and what it spent its money on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this witness was brought into a situation of providing expert testimony about documents that were signed by the deputy of Krsto Savic, and you didn't intervene then, Mr. Harhoff. And he had never seen those documents in his life, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Stop this, please. This witness was not brought in as an expert on anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I have totally completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There is no additional questions for the Court witness. We have to finish off because Judge Harhoff has to sit on another trial. Very often, the Judges on this Bench have two trials to attend, and it's exhausting, but that's just the way it is. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My apologies. We have forwarded the report to the Chamber through the legal officer, and my suggestion is that maybe Your Honours don't want to release the witness until you've had a chance to look at the document and determine whether or not you think you would want to put further questions to the witness based on this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no additional questions, no additional questions. You told us that you gave the document to the legal officer. We will look at it. Maybe the Trial Chamber made a mistake. Maybe we did obtain this document and couldn't -- didn't see it or neglected it. We'll look into this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I do not think Your Honours have received the document. That's why I forwarded it. Also, if Your Honours have any wishes for other documents, such as criminal records, for any of the witnesses, I hope Your Honours will communicate that to the Prosecution so we can assist Your Honours with any kind of records you might require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me put the question to my fellow Judge, Judge Lattanzi. I believe she had a question for the witness, an additional question. Further Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quickly, as far as you know, because maybe you know nothing about all this, but as far as you know, could you tell us whether the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, the Seseljevci, whether they were all officially members of the Serbian Radical Party or whether there were also volunteers who were not members of the SRS; maybe they joined later on, maybe they never joined? So as far as you know, do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on behalf of my fellow Judges, I thank you for coming and testifying here for the Court. Don't leave right now, because we have to drop the blinds. I wish you a safe return home. Mr. Seselj, we will resume on Tuesday, February 16, at 9.00 a.m., since there will be no hearing next week. So Tuesday, February 16, 9.00 a.m. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
